title: The Five Phases of Architectural Design
summary: The five phases of architectural design, from schematic design to construction administration: what each one produces and what carries into the next project.
body_markdown:
In the United States, the American Institute of Architects (AIA) divides an architect's work into five phases:


- Schematic design (SD)
- Design development (DD)
- Construction documents (CD)
- Bidding or negotiation
- Construction administration (CA)


Many firms add pre-design before and closeout after.


This guide explains each stage of the design process, with a focus on the role of the architectural team. It also discusses how the five architectural design phases fit into the typical stages of a construction project, best practices for managing the design process, and how Pirros helps architecture and engineering firms to design more efficiently.


## The five phases at a glance


The[AIA's definition of the architect's basic services](https://www.aia.org/resource-center/defining-the-architects-basic-services) describes five design phases:


1. **Schematic design.** What are we building, and how are we building it? Its deliverable is an approved concept, a program and a first cost estimate.
2. **Design development.** What materials are we using, and how do the systems fit together? Its deliverables are fixed materials, assemblies and consultant layouts, with outline specifications.
3. **Construction documents.** How exactly will the building be built? Its deliverable is a set a contractor can price and build from.
4. **Bidding and permitting.** Who builds it, at what cost, and is it approved? Its deliverables are a signed construction contract and an approved permit set.
5. **Construction administration.** Is the project being built as drawn? Its deliverables are a finished building and a record of what changed.


Some firms count seven phases. They add pre-design (programming, site analysis and feasibility) before schematic design, and closeout after construction administration.


## Schematic design determines the project scope


Schematic design is the first phase of design, where the architect and owner agree on what the project is and the basic form it takes. It starts with the program: the functions the building needs and the rough area of each. The architect then tests that program in study drawings that show spatial relationships, scale and form.


Schematic design is also when fundamental project research takes place. Zoning limits, code requirements and jurisdictional restrictions are analyzed here, while they are still relatively feasible to design around. Typical deliverables at this stage are a site plan, floor plans, sections, an elevation, and renderings or models, with overall dimensions and a construction cost estimated from the project's overall size.


SD should settle foundational project concepts: the structural system, the approach to the envelope, the parti. What it can leave open is execution: products, most dimensions and nearly every detail. The phase ends when the owner approves the schematic design.


Some firms run a looser concept design phase first: a few options sketched out to enable agreement on an overall direction. Schematic design is where the chosen concept becomes a drawn, dimensioned and priced proposal.


## Design development determines materials and systems


Design development turns the approved schematic design into a fully coordinated building, with its systems, materials and dimensions fixed. Structural, mechanical, electrical and plumbing layouts are determined, and the architect sets material types and the locations of doors and windows. A DD set usually carries fully dimensioned plans, sections and elevations, door and window details, and outline specifications. The phase ends with a presentation to the owner and their approval.


During DD, details are selected, even if they aren't fully drawn yet. Wall types, roof edges, window heads and floor assemblies are chosen here. A team that picks them from details the firm has already built and checked carries them into CDs almost unchanged. A team that starts from a blank sheet will often wind up drawing them twice: once to show intent in DD, and again for real in CD.


One wall section at three phases: a line and a label in SD, the layers and materials in DD, and every part, dimension and note in CD.


## Construction documents determine execution details


Construction documents are the drawings and specifications that a contractor prices and builds from, and they are the most detailed part of the plans. Once the owner approves DD, the team turns every decision into thorough instructions: plans, elevations, sections, schedules and the details for each condition the builder will meet. For what belongs in the set and how firms put one together, see our guide to[construction documents](https://www.pirros.com/blog/construction-documents) ; for the sheet types and how to read them, see[construction drawings](https://www.pirros.com/blog/construction-drawings) .


Most teams issue the set at progress milestones, often named by how complete it is: 50% CD, 90% CD and 100% CD. Each issue goes to the owner and consultants for review and coordination, and each is a chance to check the set before the next stage.


Details carry much of the effort. Every head, sill, parapet and transition the contractor will build needs a drawing, and each one has to agree with the plans, the schedules and the notes. That is why[architectural details](https://www.pirros.com/blog/architectural-detailing) are where a firm's past work saves the most time, and why a[QA/QC](https://www.pirros.com/blog/qaqc-for-revit-complete-guide) check before each issue pays for itself.


## Bidding and permitting change the set again


In the bidding or negotiation phase, the set goes out to contractors for pricing, and the owner picks a contractor and signs a construction contract. On a bid project, the architect helps prepare the bid documents, answers bidders' questions and helps the owner compare the bids. On a negotiated project, the owner works out price and scope with one contractor before the contract is signed. Permit review usually runs in parallel, and the plan reviewer's comments are ultimately incorporated as changes to the set.


This is when the set changes under deadline. Bidders' questions become addenda, plan-check comments become revisions, and a product substitution can touch notes on dozens of sheets. Add or cut a detail on a sheet and its numbering falls out of order.


On a design-bid-build job, the contractor isn't chosen until the set is complete and out for bid, so the set has to stand on its own. As Trent Piazzoni, an Associate and Project Architect at[Number TEN Architectural Group](https://www.pirros.com/customers/number-ten-architectural-group) , puts it: "The drawings need to communicate the design intent as clearly as possible, leaving as little room for misinterpretation as we can."


## Construction administration checks that a project is built as drawn


Construction administration is the architect's role during the build: answering the contractor's questions, reviewing what the contractor submits, and checking that the on-site construction matches the documents. CA services run from the construction contract until the final certificate of payment, and the owner-architect agreement sets how much of it the architect is responsible for.


A typical CA phase includes:


- Answering requests for information (RFIs) from the contractor
- Reviewing submittals and shop drawings, the fabricators' drawings of what they will make, against the design intent
- Issuing sketches and supplemental instructions when the site needs more than the set shows
- Reviewing change orders and the contractor's payment applications
- Site visits, field reports, the punch list at the end and the closeout documents


"Construction administration" is also a job title. At larger firms, a dedicated CA architect may run this phase across several projects.


CA is also where a firm learns. An RFI that exposes a sill detail that leaks is a lesson for every future project that uses the same detail.


## How the design phases fit with the phases of construction


A construction project is typically divided into six phases: initiation, design, procurement, pre-construction, construction and closeout. The architect's five phases sit inside them:


- **Initiation and feasibility** is the owner's work, often with the architect's pre-design help.
- **Design** covers schematic design, design development and construction document development.
- **Procurement** covers bidding or negotiation: the owner chooses a contractor and signs the construction contract.
- **Pre-construction** covers permitting and the contractor's buyout of the trades.
- **Construction** is construction administration for the architect.
- **Post-construction** is closeout: the punch list, record drawings and warranties.


In the UK, the[RIBA Plan of Work](https://www.riba.org/work/insights-and-resources/riba-plan-of-work/) splits the same process into eight stages, numbered 0 to 7. They line up roughly like this:


- **Stages 0 and 1, Strategic Definition and Preparation and Briefing:** pre-design
- **Stage 2, Concept Design:** close to schematic design
- **Stage 3, Spatial Coordination:** close to design development
- **Stage 4, Technical Design:** close to construction documents
- **Stage 5, Manufacturing and Construction:** construction administration
- **Stage 6, Handover:** closeout
- **Stage 7, Use:** the building in operation, beyond the AIA's basic services


Procurement isn't a stage of its own in the RIBA plan; when the contractor is appointed depends on the procurement route.


## Common problems during architectural design


- **The same details get drawn again.** A good parapet detail from a past project gets redrawn, because nobody can find the original detail.
- **DD decisions drift in CD.** The wall types picked in DD are redrawn by someone else in CD, and the two versions aren't consistent.
- **Late changes land one element at a time.** A substitution during bidding, a detail cut from a sheet, a renamed material: each is a fix by hand across many sheets, under deadline.
- **CA lessons aren't applied to future projects.** The RFI answer that fixed a leaking sill lives in an email thread, and is never reflected in an updated version of the firm's standard detail.
- **Knowledge leaves with people.** When an architect who spearheaded the project leaves the firm, the next team works without that knowledge.


## Best practices during design phases


Firms that run their design phases well treat each phase as a chance to reuse what they already know and apply new learnings to future projects.


1. **Start SD and DD from the firm's own work.** Look at past projects of the same type, climate and construction before drawing anything new.
2. **Choose details in DD from firm standards.** Settle wall types, roof edges and openings from details the firm has already vetted.
3. **Check quality at every milestone.** A review at 50% CD catches what a review at 100% CD finds too late to fix easily.
4. **Agree what each phase delivers.** Name the deliverables and the level of development for each phase in the contract, so the owner, consultants and team expect the same set.
5. **Feed CA back into the standards.** When an RFI changes a detail, update the firm's standard version too, not only the project's version.
6. **Give the standards an owner.** Someone has to decide which details become standard and keep them current, or they drift.


## Where Pirros helps


Pirros is the AI project hub for architects and engineers. It makes every detail and family your firm has drawn searchable, so each phase starts from what the firm has already solved rather than a blank sheet.


**In SD and DD, find what the firm already drew.** With[detail management](https://www.pirros.com/product/detail-management) , you describe the condition, not the file name, and Pirros searches the details from your firm's past projects, including live Revit details. The details your firm has approved as standard come first, so teams reach for the vetted version.


[Lake Flato Architects](https://www.pirros.com/customers/how-lake-flato-architects-turned-firm-history-into-everyday-speed-and-quality-with-pirros) tested Pirros with teams in late DD and early CD, which its case study describes as the phases "where pain is highest and results are most visible." Lake Flato's teams now "spend 50% less time opening models, upgrading, and previewing Revit content," and "save 5 minutes per detail found and 15 minutes per detail download."


**Before each issue, check the set.** Pirros Quality Management reviews a set against building codes, your firm's standards and the project specifications, and flags what to look at; your team decides what to change. At[Number TEN Architectural Group](https://www.pirros.com/customers/number-ten-architectural-group) , a review of a set about to go out to bid surfaced sloped glazing and safety glass requirements missing from the set, and the team carried them into the specification.


**In late CD, bidding and CA, let Mira handle the repetition.**[Mira](https://www.pirros.com/mira) , the AI agent for Revit, is free to download and works in your model with you. It handles the edits that would otherwise go one element at a time:


- "Renumber the details on this sheet." Mira reads where each viewport title sits, works out the pattern your sheets use, and draws each numbering option for you to choose before it changes anything. Detail numbers such as SIM or N.T.S. are pointed out, not overwritten.
- "Replace 'VCT' with 'LVT' in every text note." For a substitution, Mira finds every match first, asks whether each note keeps its capitalization and whether to match whole words only, then tells you how many notes will change and waits for your go-ahead.
- "Audit this view against our standards." For a detail from a consultant or another project, Mira compares its annotation styles with your firm's template and remaps what doesn't match, with ranked suggestions where it isn't sure.


Each of these skills shows what it plans to change and waits for your go-ahead. Most make the whole change as one step, so a single Ctrl+Z reverses it. Mira runs in Revit 2025 and later.


Mira replacing VCT with LVT in a set's text notes: it searches every view, asks about whole words and capitalization, and changes nothing until you approve the list.


Every project moves through the same five phases, but the firms that run them well don't start each one from scratch. They choose details in DD from what they've already built, check the set at every milestone, and carry the lessons from CA back into their standards. That's how each new project starts from everything the firm has already solved.
